claim: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness, with more than 80 million cases worldwide.
source: Glaucoma, an optic neuropathy, is the leading cause of irreversible blindness, with more than 80 million cases worldwide (Tham et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tham et al., 2014.

claim: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the most common subtype of glaucoma.
source: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), the most common subtype of the disease, is characterized by a gradual loss of retinal ganglion cells and a corresponding loss of vision.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is a major risk factor for glaucoma.
source: While the exact mechanism underlying retinal ganglion loss is not well understood, elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) is a major risk factor Coleman and Miglior, 2008
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coleman and Miglior, 2008.

claim: All current clinical treatments for glaucoma seek to sustainably lower IOP.
source: consequently, all current clinical treatments seek to sustainably lower IOP, using pharmacological, laser, and surgical means.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical practice.

claim: The success of IOP-lowering treatments is reduced by low patient adherence to medical therapies.
source: However, the success of such IOP-lowering treatments is reduced by low patient adherence to medical therapies (Reardon et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reardon et al., 2011.

claim: The success of IOP-lowering treatments is reduced by postsurgical complications.
source: However, the success of such IOP-lowering treatments is reduced by low patient adherence to medical therapies (Reardon et al., 2011), by postsurgical complications, and/or by patients becoming refractory to originally successful treatments (Heijl et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of current treatments, with citation to Heijl et al., 2002 for the refractory aspect.

claim: Patients can become refractory to originally successful glaucoma treatments.
source: However, the success of such IOP-lowering treatments is reduced by low patient adherence to medical therapies (Reardon et al., 2011), by postsurgical complications, and/or by patients becoming refractory to originally successful treatments (Heijl et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Heijl et al., 2002.

claim: The trabecular meshwork (TM) drains the majority of aqueous humor from the human eye.
source: The trabecular meshwork (TM; Figure 1) is an ocular tissue that drains the majority of aqueous humor (AH) from the human eye, and its function is a major determinant of IOP.
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical and physiological knowledge.

claim: TM function is a major determinant of IOP.
source: The trabecular meshwork (TM; Figure 1) is an ocular tissue that drains the majority of aqueous humor (AH) from the human eye, and its function is a major determinant of IOP.
evidence: This is stated as established physiological knowledge.

claim: There is an age-associated loss of TM cells which is accelerated in POAG.
source: There are a number of age- and glaucoma-associated changes in the TM, including an age-associated loss of TM cells which is accelerated in POAG (Alvarado et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alvarado et al., 1984.

claim: TM cell deficiency has been identified as a therapeutic target for IOP control in glaucoma patients.
source: This cell deficiency has been identified as a therapeutic target for IOP control in glaucoma patients, with multiple groups attempting to re-functionalize the TM by injection of stem cells into the eye to restore normal IOP homeostasis (Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013; Roubeix et al., 2015; Abu-Hassan et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017; Yun et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020; Xiong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting stem cell therapy attempts.

claim: Cell delivery to the TM has typically relied on passive transport of cells by AH outflow, leading to extremely low delivery efficiencies.
source: For example, cell delivery to the TM has typically relied on passive transport of cells by AH outflow, leading to extremely low delivery efficiencies (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: A magnetically steered cell delivery technique significantly outperforms previously used magnetic and nonmagnetic delivery techniques.
source: We have recently introduced a magnetically steered cell delivery technique which significantly outperforms previously used magnetic and nonmagnetic delivery techniques (Bahrani Fard et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work (Bahrani Fard et al., 2023).

claim: Zhou et al., 2020 reported an increase in inflammatory markers CD45 and GR1 and T-cell markers CD4 and CD3 in the iris and cornea after mesenchymal stem cell injection.
source: e.g., Zhou et al., 2020 reported an increase in the inflammatory markers CD45 and GR1 and T-cell markers CD4 and CD3 in the iris and the cornea after mesenchymal stem cell injection, likely due to off-target cell delivery.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: TMSC therapy lowers IOP and increases TM cellularity.
source: TMSC therapy lowers IOP and increases TM cellularity (Yun et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yun et al., 2018 and Xiong et al., 2021.

claim: TMSCs constitute only 2–5% of the entire TM cell population.
source: However, the scarcity of TMSCs, constituting only 2–5% of the entire TM cell population (Braunger et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Braunger et al., 2014.

claim: Mesenchymal stem cells have been used in several studies, showing a transient IOP reduction, as well as neuroprotection.
source: Alternatively, mesenchymal stem cells have been used in several studies, showing a transient IOP reduction, as well as neuroprotection (Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013; Roubeix et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013 and Roubeix et al., 2015.

claim: Manuguerra-Gagné et al. injected bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells in a rat model of IOP elevation, observing a reduction in IOP for 3 weeks.
source: For example, Manuguerra-Gagné et al. injected bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells in a rat model of IOP elevation, observing a reduction in IOP for 3 weeks (Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013.

claim: Mesenchymal stem cell therapy has established safety in clinical trials.
source: These results, together with the ease of sourcing autologous cells and the established safety of mesenchymal stem cell therapy in clinical trials (Lalu et al., 2012; Rodríguez-Fuentes et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lalu et al., 2012 and Rodríguez-Fuentes et al., 2021.

claim: iPSCs can be differentiated into iPSC-TM cells, with the differentiated cells displaying phenotypic similarity to adult TM cells.
source: Finally, iPSCs can be differentiated into iPSC-TM cells, with the differentiated cells displaying phenotypic similarity to adult TM cells (Ding et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ding et al., 2014.

claim: Intracameral injection of iPSC-TMs into a perfused porcine anterior segment POAG model restored the IOP homeostatic response.
source: Intracameral injection of iPSC-TMs into a perfused porcine anterior segment POAG model restored the IOP homeostatic response (Abu-Hassan et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abu-Hassan et al., 2015.

claim: Zhu and colleagues delivered iPSC-TMs into the anterior chambers of ocular hypertensive mice and reported increased TM cellularity due to proliferation of endogenous cells and a corresponding decrease in the IOP for up to 12 weeks after cell delivery.
source: Additionally, Zhu and colleagues delivered iPSC-TMs into the anterior chambers of ocular hypertensive mice and reported increased TM cellularity due to proliferation of endogenous cells and a corresponding decrease in the IOP for up to 12 weeks after cell delivery (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claim: Raghunathan et al., 2018 showed that when healthy TM cells are cultured on the ECM derived from glaucomatous TM cells, the healthy cells experience differential stiffening and altered expression profiles similar to the glaucomatous phenotype.
source: Raghunathan et al., 2018 showed that when healthy TM cells are cultured on the ECM derived from glaucomatous TM cells, the healthy cells experience differential stiffening and altered expression profiles similar to the glaucomatous phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Raghunathan et al., 2018.

claim: Nonhuman primate models show high anatomical and functional resemblance to humans and are the gold standard for certain preclinical studies.
source: For example, although nonhuman primate models show high anatomical and functional resemblance to humans and are the gold standard for certain preclinical studies (Friedman et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Friedman et al., 2017.

claim: Induction of ocular hypertension in nonhuman primates requires laser photocoagulation of the TM, which is very unlike TM changes seen in POAG.
source: induction of ocular hypertension requires laser photocoagulation of the TM, which is very unlike TM changes seen in POAG (Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013; Acott et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013 and Acott et al., 1989.

claim: Microbead and hypertonic saline models of ocular hypertension are distinct from human POAG pathology.
source: Microbead (Sappington et al., 2010) and hypertonic saline (Morrison et al., 1997) models of ocular hypertension are similarly distinct from human POAG pathology.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sappington et al., 2010 and Morrison et al., 1997.

claim: DBA/2 mice show TM cell loss and IOP elevation but are associated with undesirable systemic and ocular complications.
source: Commercially available DBA/2 mice show TM cell loss and IOP elevation but are associated with undesirable systemic and ocular complications (Turner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Turner et al., 2017.

claim: Transgenic MYOCY437H mice carry a glaucoma-causing point mutation in the MYOC gene and have been reported to show an accelerated loss of TM cellularity and a gradual ocular hypertension development.
source: These mice carry a glaucoma-causing point mutation in the MYOC gene and have been reported to show an accelerated loss of TM cellularity and a gradual ocular hypertension development (Zode et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zode et al., 2011.

claim: Magnetically steered delivery of hAMSCs led to a 4.5 [3.1, 6.0] mmHg or 27% reduction in intraocular pressure (IOP) for 9 months after a single dose of only 1500 cells.
source: We observed a 4.5 [3.1, 6.0] mmHg or 27% reduction in intraocular pressure (IOP) for 9 months after a single dose of only 1500 magnetically steered hAMSCs
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study, as shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The IOP reduction after hAMSC delivery was explained by increased outflow through the conventional pathway.
source: We observed a 4.5 [3.1, 6.0] mmHg or 27% reduction in intraocular pressure (IOP) for 9 months after a single dose of only 1500 magnetically steered hAMSCs, explained by increased outflow through the conventional pathway
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on outflow facility measurements presented in the study, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: hAMSC treatment was associated with a higher TM cellularity.
source: We observed a 4.5 [3.1, 6.0] mmHg or 27% reduction in intraocular pressure (IOP) for 9 months after a single dose of only 1500 magnetically steered hAMSCs, explained by increased outflow through the conventional pathway and associated with a higher TM cellularity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on TM cellularity presented in the study, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: iPSC-TM cells showed a 1.9 [0.4, 3.3] mmHg or 13% IOP reduction.
source: iPSC-TM cells were also effective, but less so, showing only a 1.9 [0.4, 3.3] mmHg or 13% IOP reduction
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study, as shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: iPSC-TM cells showed increased risk of tumorigenicity.
source: iPSC-TM cells were also effective, but less so, showing only a 1.9 [0.4, 3.3] mmHg or 13% IOP reduction and increased risk of tumorigenicity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of tumor formation in iPSC-TM treated eyes, as shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Injected cells remained detectable in the iridocorneal angle 3 weeks post-transplantation.
source: In both cases, injected cells remained detectable in the iridocorneal angle 3 weeks post-transplantation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescent imaging, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mechanism of IOP lowering is most likely paracrine signaling based on the locations of the delivered cells.
source: Based on the locations of the delivered cells, the mechanism of IOP lowering is most likely paracrine signaling.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that hAMSCs accumulated near but not within the TM, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: No meaningful IOP difference was observed between Tg-MYOCY437H mice and wild-type littermates.
source: Surprisingly, we saw no meaningful IOP difference between Tg-MYOCY437H mice (Tg group) and wild-type (WT) littermates (Figure 2; Table 1 and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IOP measurements presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Magnetically steered delivery of hAMSCs led to a marked IOP decrease in Tg animals as compared to sham injection of saline at short-, mid-, and long-term time points.
source: Despite this lack of IOP elevation in the transgenic model, magnetically steered delivery of hAMSCs led to a marked IOP decrease in Tg animals as compared to sham injection of saline at short-, mid-, and long-term time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IOP measurements presented in Figure 2 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The IOP reduction was sustained in hAMSC-treated eyes over all three time points, with no statistically significant difference between any combination of these time points.
source: The IOP reduction was sustained in hAMSC-treated eyes over all three time points, with no statistically significant difference between any combination of these time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of IOP data presented in Table 2.

claim: iPSC-TM treatment led to a reduction in IOP compared to sham injection controls at both the short- and mid-term time points, although this difference did not reach statistical significance at the latter time.
source: iPSC-TM treatment also led to a reduction in IOP compared to sham (phosphate-buffered saline [PBS]) injection controls at both the short- and mid-term time points, although this difference did not reach statistical significance at the latter time.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IOP measurements and statistical analysis presented in Figure 2 and Table 2.

claim: No significant difference in facility was found between the naïve WT and transgenic groups.
source: Specifically, no significant difference in facility was found between the naïve WT and transgenic groups
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental outflow facility measurements and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: hAMSC treatment led to a marked increase in outflow facility vs. injection controls at short-, mid-, and long-term time points.
source: while hAMSC treatment led to a marked increase in outflow facility vs. injection (sham) controls at short-, mid-, and long-term time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental outflow facility measurements presented in Figure 3 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: The percentage increases in facility due to hAMSC delivery vs. sham injection controls were similar at all time points.
source: Further, the percentage increases in facility due to hAMSC delivery vs. sham injection controls were similar at all time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental outflow facility measurements presented in Figure 3 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Groups receiving iPSC-TMs showed an increase in facility, but these differences did not reach statistical significance.
source: Groups receiving iPSC-TMs also showed an increase in facility, but these differences did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental outflow facility measurements and statistical analysis presented in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: hAMSC treatment resulted in a 2.2-fold increase in TM cellularity at the short-term time point vs. the corresponding sham injection control.
source: We observed more nuclei in eyes receiving cell transplantation, with a striking 2.2-fold increase in TM cellularity (normalized to the anterior-posterior length of the outflow tissues) after hAMSC treatment at the short-term time point vs. the corresponding (sham) injection control (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental TM cellularity measurements presented in Figure 4.

claim: The spike in TM cell density after hAMSC treatment was followed by a decline over time, reaching a 1.6-fold increase at the mid-term time point and apparently plateauing at 1.6-fold at the long-term time point.
source: Interestingly, this spike in TM cell density was followed by a decline over time, reaching a 1.6-fold increase at the mid-term time point and apparently plateauing at 1.6-fold at the long-term time point.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental TM cellularity measurements presented in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: hAMSC-treated eyes showed significantly higher cellular density vs. their injection controls at both mid-term and long-term time points.
source: Despite this modest decline, hAMSC-treated eyes showed significantly higher cellular density vs. their injection controls at both mid-term and long-term time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental TM cellularity measurements and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: Delivery of iPSC-TMs led to an increase in TM cellular density vs. sham injection controls at both short-term and mid-term time points, although these differences were more modest than seen in hAMSC-injected eyes and did not reach statistical significance.
source: Delivery of iPSC-TMs also led to an increase in TM cellular density vs. (sham) injection controls at both short-term and mid-term time points, although these differences were more modest than seen in hAMSC-injected eyes and did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental TM cellularity measurements and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: TM cellularity in iPSC-TM-treated eyes at both time points were comparable to those at the mid-term and long-term time points in hAMSC-treated eyes but were significantly different than hAMSC-treated eyes at the short-term time point.
source: Interestingly, the TM cellular densities in iPSC-TM-treated eyes at both time points were comparable to those at the mid-term and long-term time points in hAMSC-treated eyes but were significantly different than hAMSC-treated eyes at the short-term time point.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental TM cellularity measurements and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between TM cellularity and IOP for pooled data from all experimental groups (Pearson's correlation coefficient = –0.63 and p<10⁻⁷).
source: Cross-plotting normalized TM cellularity vs. IOP for pooled data from all the experimental groups (Figure 4D) showed a strong negative correlation between these two parameters, indicating an association between greater TM cellularity and lower IOP.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of TM cellularity and IOP data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: An increased deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM), and, in particular, basement membrane material (BMM), in the TM immediately adjacent to the inner wall of Schlemm's canal has been associated with ocular hypertension.
source: An increased deposition of extracellular matrix (ECM), and, in particular, basement membrane material (BMM), in the TM immediately adjacent to the inner wall (IW) of Schlemm's canal has been associated with ocular hypertension (Li et al., 2021; Overby et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021 and Overby et al., 2014.

claim: The region within the TM immediately adjacent to the inner wall of Schlemm's canal accounts for the majority of AH outflow resistance.
source: Since this region within the TM accounts for the majority of AH outflow resistance (Ethier et al., 1986)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ethier et al., 1986.

claim: Reduced amounts of BMM adjacent to the IW of Schlemm's canal were evident in transmission electron micrographs from eyes receiving hAMSCs compared to sham-injected controls at the mid-term time point.
source: Reduced amounts of BMM adjacent to the IW of Schlemm's canal were evident in transmission electron micrographs from eyes receiving hAMSCs compared to sham-injected controls at the mid-term time point (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental electron microscopy data presented in Figure 5A.

claim: En face images showed a relatively uniform distribution of cells over the entire circumference of the eye.
source: En face images showed a relatively uniform distribution of cells over the entire circumference of the eye (Figure 6A), similar to previous results with magnetically steered cells (Bahrani Fard et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data presented in Figure 6A and comparison to previous work.

claim: Sagittal sections showed an accumulation of exogenous cells deep within the iridocorneal angle.
source: Sagittal sections (Figure 6B) showed an accumulation of exogenous cells deep within the iridocorneal angle.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Strong fluorescent signals were observed within the TM in iPSC-TM-injected eyes, indicating cell integration with the target tissue.
source: Interestingly, strong fluorescent signals were observed within the TM in iPSC-TM-injected eyes, indicating cell integration with the target tissue
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Most hAMSCs accumulated close to the TM (within 50 µm), but did not enter the TM.
source: in contrast, most hAMSCs accumulated close to the TM (within 50 µm), but did not enter the TM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: More than 60% of the eyes injected with iPSC-TM cells developed tumors within a month of cell injection, typically on the iris.
source: Unfortunately, there was a very high rate of tumorigenicity in eyes receiving iPSC-TMs, with more than 60% of eyes showing large intraocular masses within a month of cell injection, typically on the iris (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations of tumor formation presented in Figure 6B.

claim: Examination of select iPSC-TM-transplanted sections by a board-certified pathologist confirmed the presence of tumors based on observation of rosettes and neuroectodermal phenotype.
source: Examination of select iPSC-TM-transplanted sections by a board-certified pathologist (HEG) confirmed the presence of tumors (Figure 7), based on observation of rosettes and neuroectodermal phenotype, characteristics also found in various tumor types, including retinoblastoma (Wippold and Perry, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by expert pathological examination and comparison to known tumor characteristics, with citation to Wippold and Perry, 2006.

claim: A high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, a hallmark of tumor malignancy, and rarefaction due to tissue necrosis were noted in iPSC-TM tumors.
source: Additionally, a high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, a hallmark of tumor malignancy (Moore et al., 2019), and rarefaction due to tissue necrosis were noted.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathological observations and citation to Moore et al., 2019.

claim: No signs of tumor growth were observed in the eyes injected with hAMSCs at the long-term time point.
source: No signs of tumor growth were observed in the eyes injected with hAMSCs at the long-term time point (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental histological observations presented in Figure 7.

claim: Magnetically steered delivery of hAMSCs led to a significant and sustained lowering of IOP, which could be almost entirely explained by improved function of the conventional outflow pathway.
source: Our major finding was that magnetically steered delivery of hAMSCs led to a significant and sustained lowering of IOP, which could be almost entirely explained by improved function of the conventional outflow pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined analysis of IOP and outflow facility measurements presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: hAMSC treatment resulted in an ~27% (4.5 mmHg) IOP reduction in eyes receiving hAMSCs vs. saline injection control eyes, which was sustained for 9 months after cell delivery.
source: Specifically, we saw an ~27% (4.5 mmHg) IOP reduction in eyes receiving hAMSCs vs. saline (sham) injection control eyes, which was sustained for 9 months after cell delivery.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IOP measurements presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: This lowering of IOP was closely related to a stable ~2.8-fold increase in outflow facility in the hAMSC treatment group vs. saline injection controls.
source: This lowering of IOP was closely related to a stable ~2.8-fold increase in outflow facility in the hAMSC treatment group vs. saline injection controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental outflow facility measurements presented in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Eyes subjected to saline injection exhibited marginally higher IOPs and lower outflow facilities on average, in comparison to the transgenic animals at baseline, but these differences lacked statistical significance.
source: Eyes subjected to saline injection exhibited marginally higher IOPs and lower outflow facilities on average, in comparison to the transgenic animals at baseline. However, due to the lack of statistical significance in these differences and the inherent age difference between the saline-injected animals and the non-injected controls at baseline, no conclusive inference can be drawn regarding the effect of saline injection.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of IOP and facility data presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Uninjected contralateral transgenic eyes (10 months of age) showed an IOP of 16.5 [15.9, 17.1] mmHg.
source: The uninjected contralateral transgenic eyes (10 months of age) showed an IOP of 16.5 [15.9, 17.1] mmHg
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IOP measurements described in the Discussion section.

claim: Contralateral hypertension has been previously reported after subconjunctival and periocular injection of dexamethasone-loaded nanoparticles.
source: Of note, contralateral hypertension has been previously reported after subconjunctival and periocular injection of dexamethasone-loaded nanoparticles (Li et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: Measured IOPs were close to 'expected IOPs' calculated from facility measurements, strongly suggesting that the majority of the IOP-lowering effect after hAMSC delivery was due to an improvement in the function of the conventional outflow pathway.
source: Our measured IOPs were close to 'expected IOPs' calculated from facility measurements, strongly suggesting that the majority of the IOP-lowering effect after hAMSC delivery was due to an improvement in the function of the conventional outflow pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of IOP and facility data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a small but consistent offset between measured and expected IOPs.
source: Despite the very close correlation between measured and expected IOPs noted above, there was a small but consistent offset between these two quantities, which may be due to several factors.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of IOP and facility data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The data strongly suggests that the IOP lowering caused by stem cell therapy is largely due to a restoration of function to the conventional outflow pathway.
source: Despite some uncertainty about the minor offset between the expected and measured IOPs, the data strongly suggests that the IOP lowering caused by stem cell therapy is largely due to a restoration of function to the conventional outflow pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined analysis of IOP and outflow facility measurements.

claim: Loss of TM cells is one of the hallmarks of POAG.
source: One of the hallmarks of POAG is loss of TM cells (Alvarado et al., 1984)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alvarado et al., 1984.

claim: Alvarado et al., 1984 showed that humans at birth have ~2.3-fold higher TM cellularity compared to a 40-year-old individual, and that this cellularity reduces sharply within the first 5 years of life.
source: Interestingly, Alvarado et al., 1984 showed that humans at birth have ~2.3-fold higher TM cellularity compared to a 40-year-old individual, and that this cellularity reduces sharply within the first 5 years of life.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Alvarado et al., 1984.

claim: An accumulation of ECM within the juxtacanalicular tissue is another feature of POAG.
source: Another feature of POAG is an accumulation of ECM within the juxtacanalicular tissue (Fuchshofer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fuchshofer et al., 2003.

claim: Increased levels of transforming growth factor-β2 (TGF-β2) in the AH of POAG patients and its role in decreasing the activity of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) suggest that the abnormal ECM deposits may be due to decreased ECM turnover.
source: Nevertheless, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β2 (TGF-β2) in the AH of POAG patients (Tripathi et al., 1994) and its role in decreasing the activity of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) suggest that the abnormal ECM deposits may be due to decreased ECM turnover (Fuchshofer et al., 2003; Tamm and Fuchshofer, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tripathi et al., 1994, Fuchshofer et al., 2003, and Tamm and Fuchshofer, 2007.

claim: hAMSC-transplanted eyes at the mid-term time point had 35% less BMM under the IW of Schlemm's canal than in saline-injected control eyes.
source: Our quantification showed that this was indeed the case: hAMSC-transplanted eyes at the mid-term time point had 35% less BMM under the IW of Schlemm's canal than in saline-injected control eyes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental BMM measurements presented in Figure 5.

claim: Li et al., 2021 reported BMM normalized length values of 0.40 [0.23, 0.57] for naïve eyes and 0.50 [0.38, 0.60] for sham-injected eyes in 2- to 3-month-old C57BL/6 mice.
source: Li et al., 2021 reported values of 0.40 [0.23, 0.57] for this quantity in naïve eyes and 0.50 [0.38, 0.60] for sham-injected (PBS containing nonconjugated polymeric nanoparticles) eyes in 2- to 3-month-old C57BL/6 mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: Overby et al., 2014 measured a BMM normalized length of 0.29 [0.16, 0.42] in 6- to 7-month-old C57BL/6 mice.
source: Overby et al., 2014 measured a BMM normalized length of 0.29 [0.16, 0.42] in 6- to 7-month-old mice from the same strain.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Overby et al., 2014.

claim: The 0.52 [0.34, 0.70] BMM normalized length measured for the sham mid-term group is consistent with previously reported values.
source: Despite our sham mid-term group being 9–11 months of age and being on a transgenic background, with no phenotypic manifestation, the 0.52 [0.34, 0.70] BMM normalized length we measured for this group is consistent with those previously reported values.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental BMM measurements with previously published data.

claim: The performance of iPSC-TMs was significantly inferior to that of hAMSCs, as quantified by several outcome measures.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the performance of iPSC-TMs was significantly inferior to that of hAMSCs, as quantified by several outcome measures
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data for IOP, facility, and cellularity between hAMSC and iPSC-TM groups.

claim: The IOP reduction after iPSC-TM cell delivery was only half that seen after hAMSC delivery.
source: most notably, the IOP reduction after iPSC-TM cell delivery was only half that seen after hAMSC delivery.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental IOP measurements presented in Figure 2.

claim: The beneficial effect of iPSC-TM treatment on TM cellularity was significantly lower than hAMSC at the short-term time point (1.4-fold vs. 2.2-fold increase).
source: The beneficial effect of iPSC-TM treatment on TM cellularity was also significantly lower than hAMSC at the short-term time point (1.4-fold vs. 2.2-fold increase)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental TM cellularity measurements presented in Figure 4.

claim: A systematic review of 1000 clinical trials involving mesenchymal stem cell transplantation finds no incidence of tumorigenicity in tissues receiving mesenchymal stem cells.
source: A body of previous literature, including a systematic review of 1000 clinical trials involving mesenchymal stem cell transplantation, finds no incidence of tumorigenicity in tissues receiving mesenchymal stem cells, suggesting an intrinsic resistance to tumor formation once positioned in the correct niche (Lalu et al., 2012; Rodríguez-Fuentes et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lalu et al., 2012 and Rodríguez-Fuentes et al., 2021.

claim: Tumorigenicity remains a concern for iPSC derivatives due to transfection with oncogenic factors, genetic aberrations during in vitro cultures, and contamination of transplants with undifferentiated cells.
source: On the other hand, tumorigenicity remains a concern for iPSC derivatives due to transfection with oncogenic factors, genetic aberrations during in vitro cultures, and contamination of transplants with undifferentiated cells (Neri, 2019; Lamm et al., 2016; Yamanaka, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Neri, 2019, Lamm et al., 2016, and Yamanaka, 2020.

claim: The iris is reported to be a favorable location for organ culture and tumor formation, with fivefold faster growth compared to subcutaneous injection.
source: Interestingly, the iris is reported to be a favorable location for organ culture and tumor formation, with fivefold faster growth compared to subcutaneous injection, and thus has previously been considered for tumorigenicity safety studies, emphasizing the importance of rigorous iPSC processing in any future treatments involving iPSC-TM cell injection into the anterior chamber (Olson and Seiger, 1972; Inagaki et al., 2022; Boone and DuPree, 1968).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Olson and Seiger, 1972, Inagaki et al., 2022, and Boone and DuPree, 1968.

claim: Both cell types were detectable in the anterior chamber 3 weeks after injection.
source: Both cell types were detectable in the anterior chamber 3 weeks after injection (Figure 6B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: iPSC-TM cells tended to better integrate with the TM tissue, whereas the hAMSCs mostly accumulated close to, but not within, the TM.
source: with iPSC-TM cells tending to better integrate with the TM tissue, whereas the hAMSCs mostly accumulated close to, but not within, the TM.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental imaging data presented in Figure 6B.

claim: The widely reported aggregation of mesenchymal stem cells immediately posttransplantation may have prevented them from entering the deeper aspects of the TM.
source: This phenomenon, which was consistently observed, may be due to the widely reported aggregation of mesenchymal stem cells immediately posttransplantation (Burand et al., 2020), which consequently prevented them from entering the deeper aspects of the TM, characterized by narrow flow channels.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and citation to Burand et al., 2020.

claim: The exogenous iPSC-TMs more directly contributed to increasing TM cellularity than did the hAMSCs due to the better integration of iPSC-TM cells into the TM.
source: Note that the exogenous iPSC-TMs more directly contributed to increasing TM cellularity than did the hAMSCs due to the better integration of iPSC-TM cells into the TM.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of cell localization and TM cellularity.

claim: Loss of signal in long-term in vivo fluorescent cell tracking is inevitable.
source: In addition, loss of signal in long-term in vivo fluorescent cell tracking is inevitable (Progatzky et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Progatzky et al., 2013.

claim: The lack of specific hAMSC homing into the TM provides important insight about the putative mechanism(s) by which these cells lowered IOP and improved AH dynamics.
source: The lack of specific hAMSC homing into the TM also provides important insight about the putative mechanism(s) by which these cells lowered IOP and improved AH dynamics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of cell localization.

claim: Du and colleagues showed that TMSCs that reach the TM co-express AQP1 and CHI3L1, indicative of their differentiation into TM cells.
source: Du and colleagues, in two studies using mice, showed that TMSCs that reach the TM co-express AQP1 and CHI3L1, indicative of their differentiation into TM cells, although quantification was not performed (Yun et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Yun et al., 2018 and Xiong et al., 2021.

claim: Zhu et al., 2016 reported a 114% increase in TM cellularity after iPSC-TM injection in MYOCY437H mice compared to saline-injected controls, yet TM-residing exogenous cells accounted for only 23% of this increase.
source: Zhu et al., 2016 reported a 114% increase in TM cellularity after iPSC-TM injection in MYOCY437H mice compared to saline-injected controls, yet TM-residing exogenous cells accounted for only 23% of this increase.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2016.

claim: Several studies report the proliferative effect of exogenous cells on the TM in terms of higher Ki-67 expression and BrdU signal, as well as an increased prevalence of Nestin+ progenitor cells.
source: This finding is consistent with several studies that report the proliferative effect of exogenous cells on the TM in terms of higher Ki-67 expression and BrdU signal, as well as an increased prevalence of Nestin+ progenitor cells (Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013, Zhu et al., 2016, and Zhu et al., 2020.

claim: Zhu et al. showed that iPSC-TMs induce significant proliferation of TM5 cells or primary TM cells carrying Ad5RSV-myocilinY437H when in co-culture, yet did not when they were co-cultured in the presence of a physical separation between iPSC-TMs and TM cells.
source: In two studies, Zhu et al. showed that iPSC-TMs induce significant proliferation of both cells from the TM5 cell line (an immortalized TM cell line) or primary TM cells carrying Ad5RSV-myocilinY437H when in co-culture, yet did not when they were co-cultured in the presence of a physical (membrane) separation between iPSC-TMs and TM cells (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhu et al., 2016 and Zhu et al., 2020.

claim: Xiong et al., 2021 conducted experiments with TMSCs and MyocY437H primary TM cells and observed no proliferative effect with or without contact between the cells.
source: Interestingly, Xiong et al., 2021 conducted similar experiments with TMSCs and MyocY437H primary TM cells and observed no proliferative effect with or without contact between the cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xiong et al., 2021.

claim: Two studies have reported the beneficial effect of injecting conditioned media from bone marrow MSCs in hypertensive rat eyes, including a significant reduction in IOP, neuroprotection, and elevated proliferation markers in the TM.
source: On the contrary, two studies have reported the beneficial effect of injecting conditioned media from bone marrow MSCs in hypertensive rat eyes, including a significant reduction in IOP, neuroprotection, and elevated proliferation markers in the TM (Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013; Roubeix et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manuguerra-Gagné et al., 2013 and Roubeix et al., 2015.

claim: The significant lowering of IOP seen after the delivery of hAMSCs and their accumulation near, but not within, the TM supports the notion that injected cells act upon the TM through their secretome.
source: In our study, the significant lowering of IOP seen after the delivery of hAMSCs and their accumulation near, but not within, the TM supports the notion that injected cells act upon the TM through their secretome.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations of IOP reduction and cell localization.

claim: The main limitation of this study was the lack of a POAG phenotype in the transgenic mouse colony.
source: The main limitation of this study was the lack of a POAG phenotype in our transgenic mouse colony.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation by the authors.

claim: MYOCY437H mice have previously been shown to exhibit an elevation in IOP and a decrease in both outflow facility and TM cellularity.
source: Even though MYOCY437H mice have previously been shown to exhibit an elevation in IOP and a decrease in both outflow facility and TM cellularity, our colony did not show any difference in those parameters compared to WT animals.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous literature on MYOCY437H mice.

claim: IOPs in WT animals lay within previously reported ranges.
source: However, this is unlikely because of the correlation between measured IOP and outflow facility in cohorts (Figure 3C) and the fact that IOPs in our WT animals lay within previously reported ranges (Zhu et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017; Overby et al., 2014; Yun et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previously published IOP values, with citations to Zhu et al., 2016, Zhu et al., 2017, Overby et al., 2014, and Yun et al., 2014.

claim: Reported IOPs for anesthetized WT C57BL/6 mice vary depending on the measurement method used, with a lower bound of ~12.5 mmHg under deep levels of injection-induced anesthesia and an upper bound of ~20 mmHg under gas-induced extra light anesthesia.
source: It should be noted that reported IOPs for anesthetized WT C57BL/6 mice vary depending on the measurement method used, with a lower bound of ~12.5 mmHg under deep levels of injection-induced anesthesia (John et al., 1997) and an upper bound of ~20 mmHg under gas-induced extra light anesthesia (Li et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to John et al., 1997 and Li et al., 2021.

claim: Goldmann's equation shows that the same percentage increase in outflow facility produces a greater magnitude of IOP lowering in a hypertensive eye vs. in a normotensive eye.
source: Additionally, Goldmann's equation (Equation 2) shows that the same percentage increase in outflow facility produces a greater magnitude of IOP lowering in a hypertensive eye vs. in a normotensive eye.
evidence: The claim is based on mathematical inference from Goldmann's equation.

claim: Magnetically steered hAMSC cell therapy has potential for long-term treatment of ocular hypertension in glaucoma.
source: We conclude that magnetically steered hAMSC cell therapy has potential for long-term treatment of ocular hypertension in glaucoma.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the combined experimental findings.

source: Outflow facility is the numerical inverse of the hydraulic resistance to AH drainage through the conventional outflow pathway.
